title: Jeremiah 6:16–30
context: Jeremiah 6:16–30 continues the LORD’s words. He invites the people to stand at the crossroads and ask for the old paths, where they will find rest for their souls, but they refuse to walk in it or to listen to the watchmen. The LORD calls the nations and the earth to witness that he will bring disaster on this people, and he rejects their incense and sacrifices because they have rejected his law. A people from the north, cruel and without mercy, is coming against the daughter of Zion; a similar description is later turned against Babylon in Jeremiah 50:41–43. In verses 24–26 a voice speaking for the people expresses terror and calls for mourning as for an only son. In the closing verses the LORD tells Jeremiah that he has made him a tester of metals among his people. The refining fails: the wicked are not removed, and they are called rejected silver, because the LORD has rejected them. Both traditions read the unit as the LORD’s final appeal and his sober verdict on a people who refuse it.

verses.text: The LORD says, “Stand in the ways and see, and ask for the old paths, ‘Where is the good way?’ and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls. But they said, ‘We will not walk in it.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the people to stand at the crossroads, ask for the old paths and the good way, and walk in it to find rest for their souls, but they refuse. Arminians see God’s sincere invitation and the people’s real refusal, which shows the seriousness of human choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the invitation is sincere and that the refusal is truly the people’s own. Both traditions note that Jesus uses the phrase "rest for your souls" in Matthew 11:29, and they read the verse as one of the clearest calls to return in the book.

verses.text: I set watchmen over you, saying, ‘Listen to the sound of the trumpet!’ But they said, ‘We will not listen!’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he set watchmen to tell them to listen to the trumpet, but they said they would not listen. Arminian readers see God providing prophets as watchmen, so the people cannot claim they were not warned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the prophets as God’s appointed means of calling his people. Both traditions compare the watchman image in Ezekiel 3:17 and 33:7, and they read the people’s refusal as deliberate.

verses.text: Therefore hear, you nations, and know, congregation, what is among them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD calls the nations and the congregation to hear and know what is among his people. Arminians see God calling witnesses to his case against Judah, which shows that his judgment is public and just.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the courtroom language as showing God’s righteousness. Both traditions read the nations as witnesses to God’s dealings with his people, a theme found elsewhere in the prophets.

verses.text: Hear, earth! Behold, I will bring evil on this people, even the fruit of their thoughts, because they have not listened to my words; and as for my law, they have rejected it.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD calls the earth to hear that he will bring disaster on this people, the fruit of their thoughts, because they rejected his words and law. Arminian readers see judgment as the natural harvest of the people’s own choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s judgment as both his act and the outworking of the people’s sin. Both traditions hold that rejecting God’s word and law lies at the root of the coming disaster.

verses.text: To what purpose does frankincense from Sheba come to me, and the sweet cane from a far country? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices are not pleasing to me.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks why incense from Sheba and sweet cane from far away come to him, saying their burnt offerings and sacrifices are not acceptable. Arminians see worship that God rejects because it is offered by people who refuse to obey him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as teaching that ritual without obedience is empty. Both traditions compare similar prophetic words in Isaiah 1:11 and Amos 5:21–22, and they hold this as shared ground. The location of Sheba is generally placed in southern Arabia.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD says, “Behold, I will lay stumbling blocks before this people. The fathers and the sons together will stumble against them. The neighbor and his friend will perish.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will lay stumbling blocks before the people, and fathers and sons, neighbors and friends will stumble and perish. Arminian readers see God’s judgment following the people’s refusal, so that they fall over the very things they chose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty even in the stumbling that judgment brings. Both traditions read the verse as describing the effects of judgment on whole families and communities, not as God tempting innocent people.

verses.text: The LORD says, “Behold, a people comes from the north country. A great nation will be stirred up from the uttermost parts of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says a people comes from the north country, a great nation stirred up from the ends of the earth. Arminians see the enemy from the north again, later identified with Babylon (25:9), approaching as God’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign rule over the nations. Both traditions note that verses 22–24 are reused almost word for word against Babylon itself in Jeremiah 50:41–43, so that the invader later faces the same kind of judgment.

verses.text: They take hold of bow and spear. They are cruel, and have no mercy. Their voice roars like the sea, and they ride on horses, everyone set in array, as a man to the battle, against you, daughter of Zion.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the invaders take bow and spear, are cruel and merciless, roar like the sea, and ride in battle array against the daughter of Zion. Arminian readers see a frightening picture of the coming army, which underscores the urgency of repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the cruelty of the enemy as part of the horror of judgment. Both traditions note that God uses the nations for his purposes without approving their cruelty, which he will later judge (compare 25:12).

verses.text: We have heard its report. Our hands become feeble. Anguish has taken hold of us, and pains as of a woman in labor.
verses.arminianNotes: A voice speaking for the people says they have heard the report, their hands are feeble, and anguish has gripped them like a woman in labor. Arminians see the terror that will come when the people finally realize the warnings were true.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image of labor pains as a common prophetic picture of sudden, unavoidable distress. Both traditions read the speaker as the people or the prophet speaking for them, and note the reuse in 50:43.

verses.text: Don’t go out into the field or walk by the way; for the sword of the enemy and terror are on every side.
verses.arminianNotes: The voice warns not to go into the field or walk on the road, because the enemy’s sword and terror are on every side. Arminian readers see the fear and danger of life under siege, when no place outside the city is safe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Both traditions note that the phrase terror on every side becomes a repeated theme in Jeremiah (compare 20:3–4, 10), and they read it as describing the reality of the coming invasion.

verses.text: Daughter of my people, clothe yourself with sackcloth, and wallow in ashes! Mourn, as for an only son, most bitter lamentation, for the destroyer will suddenly come on us.
verses.arminianNotes: The voice calls the daughter of my people to put on sackcloth, roll in ashes, and mourn bitterly as for an only son, because the destroyer will come suddenly. Arminians see a call to deep grief and repentance in the face of coming judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image of mourning for an only son as the deepest grief. Both traditions read the verse as the prophet’s lament over his people, and note that mourning here is both sorrow and a fitting response to God’s warning.

verses.text: “I have made you a tester of metals and a fortress among my people, that you may know and try their way.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah he has made him a tester of metals and a fortress among the people, to know and test their way. Arminian readers see Jeremiah’s role as exposing the true condition of the people through God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see Jeremiah’s appointment as part of God’s purpose to reveal the people’s hearts. Both traditions compare the word fortress with the LORD’s earlier promise to make Jeremiah strong against opposition (1:18).

verses.text: They are all grievous rebels, going around to slander. They are bronze and iron. All of them deal corruptly.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they are all stubborn rebels who go around slandering; they are bronze and iron, and all deal corruptly. Arminians see the testing revealing base metals rather than silver, showing how widespread the corruption has become.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as describing hearts hardened in sin. Both traditions read bronze and iron as less valuable metals mixed into what should have been pure, a picture of a people who have lost their covenant purity.

verses.text: The bellows blow fiercely. The lead is consumed in the fire. In vain they go on refining, for the wicked are not plucked away.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the bellows blow fiercely and the lead is consumed, but the refining is in vain because the wicked are not removed. Arminian readers see God’s efforts to purify his people through discipline, which they have resisted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the failed refining as showing that discipline alone does not change hearts. Both traditions read the image as a sober verdict on the people’s response, and they note that the book later promises a new covenant written on the heart (31:31–34).

verses.text: Men will call them rejected silver, because the LORD has rejected them.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says people will call them rejected silver, because he has rejected them. Arminians see the end of the testing, where those who refused to be refined are declared worthless, as the result of their persistent refusal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s rejection as a just verdict on a people who would not repent. Both traditions read the verse in light of the promise not to make a full end (5:10, 18) and the later hope of restoration in the book.
